title: 4B Setup
teaches: The 4B- (Stan Weinstein) as we trade it: after a Stage 4 decline under a falling 30-week line, a stock that has seen its low for the cycle sets a higher low on drying volume, reclaims the 50-day and pauses above it with room to run, the buy is the trade through the pause high at market once price is back above the 200-day and never more than 4% past it, the trade is short term, with the first sell a judgment on day 3 or later and no adding, and a plain 4B that is still falling is much too soon to buy.

questions.q: In Weinstein's stage legend, what does a plain 4B mean?
choices: Late in the decline: not a buy yet
A bottom is in: buy on strength
Early in the decline: sell rallies
A Stage 2 breakout on volume
questions.answer: Late in the decline: not a buy yet
questions.why: A plain 4B means late in the downtrend, and much too soon to consider buying. It is not a buy. The buy is the 4B-, the one with the minus, once its other steps are in.
questions.lesson_line: A plain 4B is not a buy. Wait for the minus.

questions.lesson_line: A clean break, too far above its average, is a pass.

wrong.Yes; the break itself is clean: A clean break can still be too stretched. Skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
wrong.Yes, but only on half size: Half size does not cure a stretch.
wrong.No; the 9 EMA is not rising yet: The rule is about distance, not slope: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.

questions.simple: No. At 12% over its 9 EMA, the stock is stretched past the 10% limit, so we skip it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a 4B- break 10 trading days ago. It sits at 0.7R and the stop has not traded.
choices: Sell; under 1R after 10 days
Hold; the stop has not traded
Widen the stop to give it room
Sell half and hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell; under 1R after 10 days
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The stop has not traded, but the time stop is its own exit. Do not widen the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not traded: The time stop is its own exit. Under 1R after 10 days, the money goes elsewhere.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade; it does not trim it.

questions.simple: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even though the stop has not traded.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: What do you do with the break?
questions.story: A clean 4B- breaks the pause high above its 200-day, but the market reading just turned Red.
choices: Stand aside; Red is mostly cash
Buy; the base is great and clean
Buy full size; Red changes nothing
Short it; Red means go short
questions.answer: Stand aside; Red is mostly cash
questions.why: Stand aside. In a Red market we are mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. This stock is above its 200-day, so it is no short. The card says Red means no new longs, and a 4B- is a long.
questions.lesson_line: A great base in a Red market still waits.

wrong.Buy; the base is great and clean: Buying against the market is the named mistake. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Buy full size; Red changes nothing: Red changes the account: we are mostly cash. A great base still waits.
wrong.Short it; Red means go short: Shorts are only below the 200-day, never above it. This stock is above its 200-day.

questions.simple: Stand aside. In a Red market we are mostly cash, so this long waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)
the card's no-new-longs line is stronger than the rulebook's guide

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: A stock has reclaimed its 50-day and paused for a week. You have not bought. Today it closes back under the 50-day.
choices: Wait for a new pause above the 50-day
Buy the dip; it is cheaper now
Wait one day, then buy as before
Buy on the first close back over it
questions.answer: Wait for a new pause above the 50-day
questions.why: Wait for a new pause. A close back under the 50-day before the trigger takes the setup off. It re-arms only after a new pause of at least 2 closes above the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Lost the 50-day, so wait for a fresh pause above it.

wrong.Buy the dip; it is cheaper now: The setup is off until a new pause forms. A dip under the 50-day is no entry.
wrong.Wait one day, then buy as before: A day of waiting is not a pause. The setup re-arms only after a new pause of at least 2 closes above the 50-day.
wrong.Buy on the first close back over it: One close back over is only the reclaim. The setup re-arms only after a new pause of at least 2 closes above the 50-day.

questions.simple: Wait for a fresh pause, because a close back under the 50-day before the buy resets the setup.

deeper.trap: A week above the 50-day does not carry over. One close back under it resets the count, and the new pause must be at least 2 closes above it.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a proposed rule the owner may change

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 1%. Buy 22.12, stop 21.49. How many shares does the risk allow?
questions.answer: 793 shares
questions.why: Risk is 1% of 50,000. Divide that by the buy minus the stop, 22.12 minus 21.49, and round down to 793 shares. The stop sets the size. The final size is the smaller of this and the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Dividing the 1% of 50,000 you risk by the gap between 22.12 and 21.49 gives 793 shares after rounding down.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A5)

choices: 793 shares
22 shares
79 shares
396 shares

wrong.22 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the buy price, not the stop distance.
wrong.79 shares: Slipped a decimal the other way and risked a tenth too little.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger.

questions.q: How do you play the open?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning it opens at 43.60.
choices: Take a third off at the open
Wait for the close
Sell all, take the gain
Take half off at the open
questions.answer: Take a third off at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open. Here 43.60 is past the 3R level at 43.00. The first trim is a third at 3R, the hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: Take the trim the open hands you.

wrong.Wait for the close: The 3R level is already passed. The rule is to take the trim at the open.
wrong.Sell all, take the gain: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Take half off at the open: The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R, not half. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.

questions.simple: Take a third off at the open, because the stock opened past the 3R level.

deeper.example: Entry 40.00 and stop 39.00 put 3R at 43.00. The day opens at 43.60, past the level, so the third comes off at the open price. The other two thirds wait for 5R, then the trail.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00. It gaps open at 38.20, and the first 30-minute low is 37.80.
choices: Out now; the loss is past the 2R cap
The new stop is the 37.80 low
Hold; gaps tend to fill in time
Sell half now; keep half for a bounce
questions.answer: Out now; the loss is past the 2R cap
questions.why: Out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, with a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here R is the gap from 40.00 to 39.00, and the 37.80 low is more than two of those under the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop has a ceiling of 2R.

wrong.The new stop is the 37.80 low: The 30-minute low is the stop only while the loss is inside 2R. This one is past it.
wrong.Hold; gaps tend to fill in time: Hope is not a rule. The gap rule has a ceiling, and this is past it.
wrong.Sell half now; keep half for a bounce: The gap rule has no half exit. The first 30-minute low is the new stop, and past 2R you get out.

questions.simple: Get out now. The first 30-minute low is past the 2R cap, so there is no new stop to hold.

deeper.example: Bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00. The stock gaps to 38.20 and the first 30-minute low is 37.80. That low sits more than 2R down, past the ceiling, so it cannot be the new stop. Had it held inside 2R, it would have been.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You hold the last third of a fast mover after both trims. Today it closes under its 10-day.
choices: Sell the last third on that close
Hold until the 50-day breaks down
Move the stop down to the 50-day
questions.answer: Sell the last third on that close
questions.why: Sell the last third. A fast mover trails the 10-day, and we sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: The trail is a close under the 10-day. Sell it.

wrong.Hold until the 50-day breaks down: The trail is the 10-day for a fast mover, not the 50-day.
wrong.Move the stop down to the 50-day: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.q: How do you answer your friend?
questions.story: Your 4B- trade is working. A friend says to add along the way, as some traders do.
choices: No; one price, one stop, no adds
Yes; add on each higher low
Yes, but add half the size
No; sell half to lock gains
questions.answer: No; one price, one stop, no adds
questions.why: No. Size from the stop, with one price, one stop and no adding along the way. Adding to it on the way up is a named mistake. The trade grows through its trims and trail, not through adds.
questions.lesson_line: Full size once. A winner is not a reason to add.

wrong.Yes; add on each higher low: Adding to it on the way up is the named mistake.
wrong.Yes, but add half the size: A smaller add is still an add with a second price and a second stop.
wrong.No; sell half to lock gains: Selling half early is not the answer to an add. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 at the earliest, and the rest trails.

questions.simple: No. We size from the stop once and never add along the way, even when the trade works.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You are up 4R in four days on a vertical, wide-range burst.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add; it is going parabolic
Hold it all; the trail will handle it
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is for selling into; how much is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical burst is for selling into.

wrong.Add; it is going parabolic: Adding is the named mistake, and a burst is for selling into.
wrong.Hold it all; the trail will handle it: The trail catches the turn late. A burst is the moment to bank a big part.

questions.q: Our position can be up to 5% of the stock's average daily volume.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The cap is 1% of a stock's average daily volume, not 5%. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the stock's volume, not just the stop.
questions.simple: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: How does the market change the buy?
questions.story: After a broad market decline the index turns up. A stock is among the first in its group to reclaim its 50-day.
choices: Good; start with a few positions
Wait; the market must make a new high
Go all in on this one
No change; judge the stock alone
questions.answer: Good; start with a few positions
questions.why: Good conditions. The card says the best turns come after a broad market decline, once the market itself turns back up. After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work.
questions.lesson_line: A market turning up is the wind behind the turn.

wrong.Wait; the market must make a new high: The best turns come when the market itself turns back up, not after a new high.
wrong.Go all in on this one: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work.
wrong.No change; judge the stock alone: The market matters. The card wants a Green or Yellow reading, and it says the best turns come once the market itself turns back up.

questions.simple: Good setting: the market is turning up, so start with a few positions and add only as they work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68)
fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: Your 4B- stalls after the buy and drifts back toward the old low. A friend says to hold it as an investment.
choices: Sell by the rules; it is a trade
Hold it; a long-term bottom
Add shares; it is cheaper
Move the stop lower for room
questions.answer: Sell by the rules; it is a trade
questions.why: Sell by the rules. A 4B- is a short-term trade on our trims, not an investment. Holding it back down into Stage 4 is the named mistake. A stalled trade exits on its stop or its time stop.
questions.lesson_line: Do not turn a short-term trade into an investment.

wrong.Hold it; a long-term bottom: Holding a short-term trade back down into Stage 4 is the named mistake.
wrong.Add shares; it is cheaper: Adding to it is a named mistake. One price, one stop, no adds.
wrong.Move the stop lower for room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Moving it lower turns a planned loss into a hope.

questions.simple: Sell by the rules, because a 4B- is a short-term trade and we never hold a stock back in Stage 4.

deeper.trap: The friend's story sounds patient, but it changes the trade. A 4B- is a short-term play, and a stalled one exits on the stop or the time stop. Hope is not an exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)
fixed before

questions.q: The stop traded. How should we read that loss?
questions.story: You bought a 4B- on the trigger at 12.99, stop 12.59. It followed a 37.5% decline, a higher low and a 12-day pause. The next session fell to 12.48.
choices: A planned loss; the stop worked
A stop that was set too tight
A buy that came in too late
Proof the 4B- does not work
questions.answer: A planned loss; the stop worked
questions.why: A planned loss. The stop is the plan, and the stop-out was the planned loss of 3.1% (12.99 to 12.59). The next session fell to 12.48 and took the stop. Judge the plan, not the outcome.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out can be the plan working. The stop makes the loss small.

wrong.A stop that was set too tight: The stop came from the day's low, as our stop rule says, and it only moves up. Calling it too tight after a loss is how stops get widened.
wrong.A buy that came in too late: The buy was on the trigger, the trade over the pause high. That is not a chase.
wrong.Proof the 4B- does not work: One loss proves nothing. Our dossier calls this the plain case of a correct 4B- that lost.

questions.simple: It was a planned loss, because the stop did its job and kept the loss small.

deeper.trap: A stop-out is not proof of a bad setup. Here the next session's low of 12.48 was under the 12.59 stop, so the exit happened as planned. Do not widen a stop after the fact. It only moves up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
the widest allowed stop is a held decision (D-005)
fixed before

questions.q: After the first stop-out, when do you buy again?
questions.story: Bought at 213.22 with the stop at 210.32. It followed a 39% drop to the March 2020 low, a higher low and a 13-day pause. The next day took the 1.4% stop.
choices: Only when it triggers again
At once; it is the same setup
Only at a lower price than before
Only after a full week of waiting
questions.answer: Only when it triggers again
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. META's second trigger on 2020-06-10 also stopped. The real move came from a third base.
questions.lesson_line: This setup can fail twice. Only a new trigger buys it again.

wrong.At once; it is the same setup: After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
wrong.Only at a lower price than before: The price level is not the rule. Buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.
wrong.Only after a full week of waiting: The rule sets no waiting period. A new trigger is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.

questions.simple: Buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a brand new trade with its own stop.

deeper.example: META, 2020: buy 213.22, stop 210.32, stopped the next session. The second trigger on 2020-06-10 also stopped. The real move came from a third base.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: What grade cue flagged this one?
questions.story: MSFT, 2001: a 66% Stage 4 decline, a 92-session base, an 18-day pause. The break reached a fraction of 1R, then the stop.
choices: A falling 200-day over the trade
The pause was too long
The base was too short
questions.answer: A falling 200-day over the trade
questions.why: A falling 200-day over the trade. The long averages should be flat or turning, not still falling steeply.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the long averages. A falling 200-day is overhead supply.

wrong.The pause was too long: An 18-day pause is inside the 5 to 20 sessions that did best.
wrong.The base was too short: A 92-session base is long. The falling long average was the cue.

questions.q: Which check could have kept you out?
questions.story: Two 4B- triggers in a bear market, months apart. Each looked clean, and each stopped the next session.
choices: The market reading
A tighter stop
A bigger position
questions.answer: The market reading
questions.why: The market reading. Two 4B- triggers in the 2008 bear were both stopped without trading above the entry. Buying against the market is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Forest first, then the trees. Check the market.

wrong.A tighter stop: A tighter stop would have been hit even sooner. The missing filter was the market.
wrong.A bigger position: More size on a losing setup only loses more.

questions.q: Is it a 4B-?
questions.story: The day before the trigger. A stock drops 34% from its high. At the cycle low the 150-day was rising: 528.74 against 521.41 twenty sessions earlier.
choices: No; a pullback in an uptrend
Yes; the drop is deep enough
Yes; price sat under the 150-day
No; it is a plain 4B, not a 4B-
questions.answer: No; a pullback in an uptrend
questions.why: No. At the cycle low the 150-day was rising: 528.74 against 521.41 twenty sessions earlier. A 4B- needs a falling 150-day first. A 34% drop under a rising 150-day is a pullback in an uptrend, so a Remount or a pullback buy, not a Stage 4 turn. The 150-day is not drawn on the chart; its two readings are in the story.
questions.lesson_line: Read the 150-day at the low before you name it.

wrong.Yes; the drop is deep enough: A deep drop is not a Stage 4. The 150-day was rising at the low.
wrong.Yes; price sat under the 150-day: Price under the 150-day is only half the test. The 150-day also has to be falling at the low, and here it was rising.
wrong.No; it is a plain 4B, not a 4B-: A plain 4B is late in a Stage 4 decline. Here the 150-day was rising at the low, so there is no Stage 4 to be late in.

questions.simple: No, because the 150-day was rising at the low, so this is a pullback in an uptrend and not a Stage 4 turn.

deeper.trap: Depth fools people. A drop of 34% looks like a Stage 4, but the 150-day tells the stage. Read it at the low. If it was rising, this is a pullback in an uptrend.

reasons: rests on figures read from our own daily bars
fixed before

questions.q: Is that a real higher low?
questions.story: A stock rallies off its cycle low to a high 4.1% above it. It then pulls back to a low 3.5% above the cycle low.
choices: No; too small a rally before it
Yes; 3.5% clears the 3% step
No; 3.5% is too shallow to be real
Yes; it sits above the cycle low
questions.answer: No; too small a rally before it
questions.why: No. Our working rule needs a rally of 5% or more before the higher low. Here the best high off the low was only 4.1% above it. The step itself is fine: 3.5% clears the 3% minimum.
questions.lesson_line: A higher low needs a 5% rally before it.

wrong.Yes; 3.5% clears the 3% step: The step is only one test. The rally of 5% or more before the higher low is missing, since the best high was just 4.1% above the low.
wrong.No; 3.5% is too shallow to be real: The step test is at least 3%, and 3.5% passes it. What fails is the rally before it.
wrong.Yes; it sits above the cycle low: Above the cycle low is not enough. A rally of 5% or more has to come before it, and the best high was just 4.1% above the low.

questions.simple: No. The rally before the higher low was only 4.1%, under the 5% we want, even though the 3.5% step clears 3%.

deeper.trap: These numbers are made up on purpose. A step of 3.5% passes one test. The rally before it is missing: the best high off the low was just 4.1% above it.

a proposed number the owner may change

questions.q: Does our earnings rule allow that buy?
questions.story: A stock closes back over its 50-day on 2022-07-18, and you want to buy it. The company reports after the close on 2022-07-19.
choices: No; too close to the report
Yes; the reclaim was clean
Yes; it came before the report
No; the 200-day comes first
questions.answer: No; too close to the report

A buy on the 18th comes the day before the report. A clean chart does not move the window. The rule guards against the risk of the report, and it does not judge a trade by how the report turned out.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy, even on a clean chart.

wrong.Yes; the reclaim was clean: A clean reclaim does not move the earnings window.
wrong.Yes; it came before the report: Buying before the report is exactly what the window bans. We take no new buy in the 3 days before one.
wrong.No; the 200-day comes first: The story says nothing about the 200-day. What it gives is the report date, the next day.

questions.simple: No, because a buy on 2022-07-18 is the day before the report, and we take no new buy in the 3 days before one.

deeper.trap: A clean chart is not a free pass. The rule looks at the report date, not at how clean the base looks. Check the date before every buy.

questions.q: Write the plan.
questions.story: 78 sessions off a December low, a February higher low, and a 19-day pause above a turning 50-day. Today it trades over the pause high.
choices: Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, first sell day 3+
Buy 49.99, stop 45.00, hold it all
Wait for a Stage 2 breakout instead
Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, add on each dip
questions.answer: Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, first sell day 3+
questions.why: Buy at market, 49.99, once price trades over the pause high. Stop 49.05, 1.9% away. The first sell is a judgment call, usually day 3 at the earliest. One price, one stop, no adding.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Buy 49.99, stop 45.00, hold it all: The stop here sat 1.9% away; 45.00 is far wider. And the plan needs a first sell and a trail.
wrong.Wait for a Stage 2 breakout instead: That is a different trade. This is the 4B-, the short-term play.
wrong.Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, add on each dip: The entry and stop are right, but adding on dips breaks the plan: one price, one stop, no adding along the way.

questions.simple: Buy at market over the pause high with the stop at 49.05, and wait until day 3 to make the first sell.

deeper.example: NUS had a December low, a February higher low, three months of flat 150- and 200-day lines, then a 19-day pause above a turning 50-day. The buy was 49.99 with the stop at 49.05, 1.9% away. Write the plan before the open: entry, stop, first sell.

reasons: numbers read from our own bars (dossier)
entry trigger rests on held decision D-003
stop width rests on held decision D-005

questions.q: Which gets the bigger size?
questions.story: Two 4B- breaks. A: a clean higher low on light volume, a tight pause on a flat 50-day, the group and market turning up. B: a steeply falling 50-day, and a group and market not turning up.
choices: A; stronger base and backdrop
B; a steep 50-day has more upside
Equal; both broke the pause high
Neither; the stop sets the size
questions.answer: A; stronger base and backdrop
questions.why: A. Its cues line up. It has a clean higher low on light volume and a tight pause on a flat 50-day. The group and market are turning up too. That is the A+ end. B's steeply falling 50-day is a B- cue. We size B- or lower grades down.
questions.lesson_line: Same setup, different grade. The base and the backdrop set the size.

wrong.B; a steep 50-day has more upside: A steeply falling 50-day is a B- cue, not extra upside. We size B- or lower grades down.
wrong.Equal; both broke the pause high: Both broke the pause high, but the grade, not the break, sets the size. A has the cues of an A+ and B has a B- cue.
wrong.Neither; the stop sets the size: The stop sets the base size, but we size B- or lower grades down. So the grade still moves the size.

questions.simple: A gets the bigger size. Its base and backdrop are strong, while B shows a weak cue and none of the strong ones.

deeper.trap: Both broke the pause high, so both look the same on a screen. The difference is what sits behind the break. A clean base and a rising backdrop earn size, and a weak base earns less.

reasons: grades rest on card judgment with no stated thresholds
the flat 50-day number is held (D-070)
fixed before

questions.q: How do you read that result?
questions.story: You take five 4B- trades by the rules. Four stop out, and one runs for 5R.
choices: Normal; this setup loses often
Broken; the setup does not work
Wrong stops; they should be wider
Bad luck; a good setup wins most
questions.answer: Normal; this setup loses often
questions.why: Normal. In our test above the 200-day, 22.2% of 1,110 hits reached 3R and 13.9% reached 5R. So most hits never reached 3R, and four stops in five is ordinary. That is a base rate for the rule, not a promise for any one trade.
questions.lesson_line: Most 4B- hits never reach 3R. Judge the setup over many trades.

wrong.Broken; the setup does not work: Four stops in five fits our test, where only 22.2% of hits reached 3R. That is the base rate, not a broken setup.
wrong.Wrong stops; they should be wider: Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low, set before the buy. Widening it to dodge stop-outs breaks that rule, and the shares shrink.
wrong.Bad luck; a good setup wins most: Our test shows the base rate: only 22.2% of hits reached 3R. Losing often is normal for this setup, not bad luck.

questions.simple: That is normal: in our test only 22.2% of hits reached 3R, so four stops in five is ordinary.

deeper.counter: The hit rate alone says little. Winners are sold into strength, and each loss is held to the stop. Judge the setup over many trades, not five.

one cited fact only (our scan)
rests on the 200-day treatment held in D-009

questions.q: In Bulkowski's own trades, Stage 4 buys made money about 24% of the time.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Bulkowski's own Stage 4 buys made money 24% of the time, so a 4B- is a low-hit-rate trade that lives on small stops and trims.
questions.lesson_line: Buying near a Stage 4 low is a low-odds trade. Trade it small and short.

questions.q: A washout, a higher low, a pause over the 50-day. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; it is above the 200-day
Pass; the 200-day is overhead
Pass; no real higher low
Take it; washouts bounce
questions.answer: Take it; it is above the 200-day
questions.why: Take it. A spring washout, a higher low, and an 11-day pause that walked up through the 50, 150 and 200-day lines. The prior close was above the 200-day, so the no-longs-under-it rule does not apply. It then ran to 5R in 9 sessions. The other checks still apply, and one winner proves nothing about the next.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day first, then the base. Both passed here.

wrong.Pass; the 200-day is overhead: Look again: price sits above the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass; no real higher low: Look again: the second low sits well above the first.
wrong.Take it; washouts bounce: A washout alone is not a setup. This one has a higher low, a pause over the 50-day and a prior close above the 200-day.

questions.q: A deep decline, a higher low, a 50-day reclaim. Is it above the 200-day? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; it is still under the 200-day
Take it; the base is textbook
Take it; the higher low is big
Pass; it is a plain 4B, still falling
questions.answer: Pass; it is still under the 200-day
questions.why: Pass. The close was 10.2% under the 200-day the day before the trigger. A 50% decline, a 12% higher low and a 50-day reclaim can all be right. The trade is still not ours. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. Only indexes and a few special ETFs get an exception.
questions.lesson_line: The shape is not enough. For a stock, the 200-day decides.

wrong.Take it; the base is textbook: A good-looking base does not matter when the close is under the 200-day. That rule comes first.
wrong.Take it; the higher low is big: A big higher low does not lift a close over the 200-day.
wrong.Pass; it is a plain 4B, still falling: A higher low and a 50-day reclaim put it past the plain 4B stage. The reason to pass is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass. The close is still under the 200-day, and we do not buy stocks under it.

deeper.trap: The shape looks complete. A 50% decline, a 12% higher low and a 50-day reclaim, yet the close was still 10% under the 200-day. Check the 200-day before you admire the base. Shape never overrides the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and held decision D-009
numbers read from our own bars (dossier)

questions.q: Which one stays on our list today?
questions.story: Four candidates today. A: still making new lows. B: the close is under the 200-day. C: a higher low, a pause over the 50-day, 3R of room. D: reports in 2 days.
choices: A; it is still making new lows
B; its close is under the 200-day
C; higher low, pause, 3R of room
D; it reports in just two days
questions.answer: C; higher low, pause, 3R of room
questions.why: C. A plain 4B still making new lows, a close under the 200-day and a report inside 3 sessions each rule one out. C has the higher low and 3R of room. C still has to clear its other gates before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Run every gate. One failure ends it.

wrong.A; it is still making new lows: A stock still making new lows is a plain 4B, much too soon to buy.
wrong.D; it reports in just two days: A report inside 3 sessions ends it.

questions.simple: C. The other three each fail a gate: A is a plain 4B, B is under the 200-day, D reports within 3 sessions.

deeper.trap: C is only the survivor of this list. It still has to clear the rest. It needs a close above the 200-day, the 50-day reclaim and a trigger over the pause high. Then the buy must be no more than 4% past the trigger.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones ___.
questions.answer: work

questions.q: Do you take the third one?
questions.story: A broad selloff ends and the market reading turns Green again. You hold two 4B- trades, both past their first trim. A third 4B- triggers.
choices: Yes; the first two are working
No; wait for a new index high
Yes, by adding to the first two
No; three at once is too many
questions.answer: Yes; the first two are working
questions.why: Yes. After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. Your first two are past their first trim, so they are working. A third position is a new trade with its own stop, not an add to the first two.
questions.lesson_line: Add positions, not shares. Let the first ones prove the turn.

wrong.No; wait for a new index high: Our rule starts positions as the reading turns Green again. It does not wait for a new index high.
wrong.Yes, by adding to the first two: That adds to a trade. Our plan is one price, one stop, no adding along the way.
wrong.No; three at once is too many: The plan starts with a few positions and adds more as the first ones work. They are working, so a third is the plan.

questions.simple: Yes, take it, because the first two are working and the plan adds new positions only as the first ones work.

deeper.counter: Add positions, not shares. A third name spreads the plan across trades. Adding to a winner means a second price and a second stop, and our plan is one price, one stop, no adding along the way.

questions.q: Which stock earns the group cue in our rule?
questions.story: Two stocks sit in one group, which is basing too. Both show the same higher low and pause above the 50-day. Stock A reclaimed its 50-day in the first week of the group's turn. Stock B reclaimed it weeks later, after most of the group.
choices: Stock A; it turned with the leaders
Stock B; it waited for the group
Neither; the order is not part of it
Both; a basing group is enough
questions.answer: Stock A; it turned with the leaders
questions.why: Stock A. The group cue in our rule is a group that is basing too, with the stock among the first in it to reclaim its 50-day. Stock B reclaimed it weeks later, after most of the group. It is a cue that helps, not a rule that ends Stock B's setup.
questions.lesson_line: In a basing group, the early reclaimers earn the cue.

wrong.Neither; the order is not part of it: The cue is about the order. The stock should be among the first in the group to reclaim its 50-day.
wrong.Stock B; it waited for the group: Stock B came late, after most of the group. The cue asks for a stock among the first to reclaim its 50-day.
wrong.Both; a basing group is enough: A basing group is only half the cue. The stock must also be among the first in it to reclaim its 50-day, and Stock B came late.

questions.simple: Stock A earns the cue because it reclaimed its 50-day among the first in a group that is basing too.

deeper.trap: Being late is not a veto. This is a cue, not a gate, so Stock B can still be a valid setup. It just does not earn this cue.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)

questions.q: Which picture of the 150-day and 200-day lines is the better cue?
choices: Flat, or turning over the trade
Falling steeply, far below
No difference to the grade
The 150 crossing the 200-day
questions.answer: Flat, or turning over the trade
questions.why: Flat, or turning. Our card wants the 150-day and 200-day lines flat or turning over the trade, not still falling steeply.
questions.lesson_line: Flat or turning long averages are the better picture. A steep fall is not.

wrong.Falling steeply, far below: The card wants the lines flat or turning, not still falling steeply. A steep fall is the weaker picture.
wrong.No difference to the grade: It is a cue that counts. Flat or turning lines are the better picture.
wrong.The 150 crossing the 200-day: The card asks for the 150-day and 200-day lines flat or turning over the trade, not for a cross.

questions.simple: Flat or turning long averages are the better picture, and a steep fall is a weaker one.

reasons: the card cue plus one web quote (x11) from a page that could not be re-opened
proposed card cue

questions.q: A steeply falling 200-day line cancels a 4B- on our card.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The card calls flat or turning lines a cue, not a veto. Lines still falling steeply are the weaker picture, but they do not cancel the setup. The close still has to be above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A falling long average is a weaker cue, not a rule that ends the setup.
questions.simple: False. A steeply falling 200-day is a weaker cue, not a veto, though the close must still be above it.

deeper.counter: A cue is not a gate, but a gate sits beside it. A 200-day can fall and still sit under price. If price is under it, the rule of no longs under the 200-day ends the trade, whatever the cue says.

reasons: proposed card cue
x11 quote from a page that could not be re-opened

questions.q: Do you buy now?
questions.story: Pre-market, a 4B- stock trades through its pause high of 20.00. The open is an hour away.
choices: No; wait for regular hours
Yes, with a market order
Yes, with a limit at 20.00
No; wait a day to see it hold
questions.answer: No; wait for regular hours
questions.why: No. Our entry is a market order once the trigger trades, and only during regular hours. No new buys outside regular trading hours, so a pre-market print is not a buy.
questions.lesson_line: Market order, regular hours only. A pre-market print is not a buy.

wrong.Yes, with a market order: A market order is our order type, but pre-market is outside regular hours.
wrong.Yes, with a limit at 20.00: Our entries are market orders, and pre-market is outside regular hours.
wrong.No; wait a day to see it hold: There is no wait-a-day step. Our entry is a market order once the trigger trades during regular hours.

questions.simple: No. We buy with a market order once the trigger trades in regular hours, never pre-market.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)
the trigger itself is the card's default

questions.q: Your planned stop level lands on exactly 25.00. Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under 25.00
Right on 25.00
A few cents over 25.00
A dollar under 25.00
questions.answer: A few cents under 25.00
questions.why: A few cents under 25.00. Our card keeps the stop off a round number: a few cents under it, not on it. Our default stop is also a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under the round number, never right on it.

wrong.Right on 25.00: Not on a round number. The stop sits a few cents under it.
wrong.A few cents over 25.00: That puts the stop above the level instead of under it. A long stop sits a few cents under.
wrong.A dollar under 25.00: A few cents is the gap. A full dollar widens the stop and shrinks the size.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under 25.00, not right on the round number.

reasons: proposed card line c42 plus the rulebook's default stop (A3)

questions.q: Our card puts the stop right on the nearest round number.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The card says not on a round number: a few cents under it. The default stop for a long is a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under the round number, not on it.
questions.simple: False. Our stop sits a few cents under a round number, not right on it.

questions.q: What is wrong with that plan?
questions.story: You buy a 4B- and plan to sell by hand if it trades under your stop level. Nothing is entered with your broker.
choices: Every position needs a real stop order
Nothing; you will be watching the screen
An alert is enough if you act fast
Place the stop after the first trim
questions.answer: Every position needs a real stop order
questions.why: A stop kept in your head is not a stop. Every position has a real stop order with the broker. The stop comes first, and it only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Place the order. A stop in your head is not a stop.

wrong.Nothing; you will be watching the screen: Watching is not an order. The stop sits with the broker even when you look away.
wrong.An alert is enough if you act fast: An alert is not an order. The rule is a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Place the stop after the first trim: Stop first: the stop sets the size, so every position has its real stop order from the start.

questions.simple: Every position needs a real stop order with the broker, because a stop in your head is not a stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: Our stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A real stop order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Real order, with the broker. It only moves up.

questions.q: By default, on a steadier mover we trail what is left under the 20 EMA, not the 9 EMA.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A steadier mover trails the 20 EMA, and a fast mover trails the 9 EMA. We sell on a close below the line, not before it.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier mover, 20 EMA. Sell on the close below.
questions.simple: True. Steadier movers trail the 20 EMA and fast movers trail the 9 EMA, selling on a close below.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You hold two thirds after the 3R trim. In three days the stock goes parabolic, 4.5R up and far over its 10-day.
choices: Sell a big part of it into the move
Hold it all until a 10-day close
Add to it while it keeps running
Wait for a red day, then sell some
questions.answer: Sell a big part of it into the move
questions.why: Sell a big part into the burst. A climax run on your own long is sold into, and how much is a judgment call. Do not add: one price, one stop, no adding along the way.
questions.lesson_line: A parabolic burst is for selling into. How much is your call.

wrong.Hold it all until a 10-day close: The trail catches the turn late. A parabolic burst is the moment to sell a big part.
wrong.Add to it while it keeps running: No adding along the way: one price, one stop. A burst is for selling into.
wrong.Wait for a red day, then sell some: The card says sell a big part into the run, not after it turns.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, since a climax run is for selling into.

deeper.trap: The trail feels safe because it is a rule, but it fires on a close under the 10-day, after the burst has run. The burst is the moment to bank a big part. The trail then handles what is left.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)

questions.q: Buy the open?
questions.story: The pause high is 40.00. The stock gaps open at 42.00.
choices: Pass; it is already too far up
Buy at market; it is strong
Buy half size at the open
Set a limit at 40.00 and wait
questions.answer: Pass; it is already too far up
questions.why: Pass. The open at 42.00 is more than 4% above the pause high of 40.00, and the cap is 4%. We skip a long that is already more than 4% above its trigger level. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.simple: Pass, because 42.00 is more than 4% above the 40.00 pause high, and we never buy more than 4% past it.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the pause high is no trade.

wrong.Buy at market; it is strong: Past 4% the stop stays far away and the shares shrink. That is a chase.
wrong.Buy half size at the open: Half of a chase is still a chase. The line is 4%.
wrong.Set a limit at 40.00 and wait: Our entries are market orders, and the trigger already traded at the open. A resting limit at the old pause high is not the plan.

deeper.trap: A gap above the line is not a gift. The line is 4% above the trigger level however the stock gets there, so a strong open does not move it. Skip the trade and wait for the next trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
replaces q21

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: You would buy at 50.00 with the stop at 48.50. The falling 150-day sits at 52.00. The 200-day is below your entry.
choices: Pass; too little room overhead
Take it; the 150-day breaks
Take it; over the 200-day
Pass; no longs under 150-day
questions.answer: Pass; too little room overhead
questions.why: Pass. Our working rule wants at least 3R from the entry to the nearest overhead level. The risk is the buy minus the stop. The falling 150-day sits above the buy by only a little more than that risk, far short of 3R.
questions.simple: Pass, because the falling 150-day sits just above the buy, which leaves far less than the 3R of room we want.
questions.lesson_line: A wall just overhead is no trade. Count the room.

wrong.Take it; the 150-day breaks: Buying right under a falling long average with less than 3R of room is the named mistake. A hoped-for break is not room.
wrong.Take it; over the 200-day: Being over the 200-day clears one gate, not the room. The falling 150-day is just overhead, and we want at least 3R.
wrong.Pass; no longs under 150-day: The no-long line is the 200-day, not the 150-day. The reason to pass is the room, which is under the 3R we want.

reasons: a proposed number the owner may change
replaces q33

questions.q: What does our card say to do now?
questions.story: Your 4B- is up 4R, and you still hold two thirds. The last three days all closed up. The last two opened on gap ups, and range and volume grew each day.
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Hold it all and let the trail work
Add a little while it is strong
Wait for the 5R trim, then sell
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Three straight up days, gap ups, and wider ranges on rising volume check the boxes of our parabolic burst. On our card a climax run is sold into, and how much is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Up days, gap ups, wider ranges, rising volume: that burst is for selling into.

wrong.Hold it all and let the trail work: The trail sells only on a close under its line. Our card sells a big part into a climax run instead.
wrong.Add a little while it is strong: One price, one stop, no adding along the way. A climax run is for selling into, not buying.
wrong.Wait for the 5R trim, then sell: At 4R the 5R trim has not come yet. Our card does not wait for it: sell a big part into a climax run.

questions.simple: When your winner bursts straight up for days on gaps and rising volume, sell a big part into it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)
the burst signs are B26's parabolic burst, read as the climax run C34 names
